title: How To Move Your Business Online in 2027
summary: Moving your business online can help you reach new audiences, reduce certain overheads, and track customer data. Learn how.
body_markdown:
A physical business without an online presence may miss out on potential customers. Moving your business online gives customers another way to find you, whether your digital store replaces physical operations or runs alongside them. In 2025 alone,[186 million](https://cdn.shopify.com/static/the-entrepreneur-effect/the-entrepreneur-effect-report.pdf) people bought from a Shopify store for the first time. That’s roughly six new first-time buyers every second.


When the pandemic shut down Bagels on Greene’s in-person catering business, second-generation owner Amit Mahtani saw an opportunity to add an online sales channel to the Montreal shop. “We didn’t have an online presence,” Mahtani says on an episode of the[Shopify Masters podcast](https://www.shopify.com/blog/bagels-on-greene-product-and-storefront-expansion) . Launching an ecommerce platform through Shopify opened up new customer discovery: “A lot of the new people that have come into the business have looked us up.”


Read on to learn about the benefits of creating an online presence for your business, and a step-by-step guide to getting it done.


## Benefits of moving your business online


- Reach customers beyond your physical location
- Introduce your business in new markets
- Sell round the clock
- Reduce overheads
- Get data you can act on


Online shopping is growing year over year. US ecommerce reached[$340.2 billion](https://www.census.gov/retail/ecommerce.html) in the second quarter of 2026, up 12.2% from 2025. Here are a few benefits of moving your business online:


### Reach customers beyond your physical location


An online store makes your business accessible to customers beyond those who walk past your local business or live nearby. This is especially valuable for businesses with a niche audience—a principle Chris Anderson documented in his 2006 book[The Long Tail](https://www.wired.com/2004/10/tail/) , which showed how online retail allows specialty products to find viable customer bases by aggregating demand across geographies that would be too thin to support a physical store. A business with limited local demand may still find enough customers nationwide or overseas to build a sustainable storefront.


### Introduce your business in new markets


Selling online lets you meet demand in other regions and areas without committing to the project of a new storefront. Offering shipping to select destinations where you expect customer interest can help you decide where to expand physically.


### Sell round the clock


Unlike a physical storefront, an ecommerce store doesn’t close at the end of the day. Unlike an offline business, your site keeps taking orders overnight, on weekends, and during holidays. That means revenue continues to come in even when you’re not actively working, giving you the flexibility to spend regular business hours on tasks like[sourcing](https://www.shopify.com/blog/product-sourcing-apps) ,[marketing](https://www.shopify.com/blog/topics/marketing) , or planning your next[product launch](https://www.shopify.com/blog/product-launch) .


Jonathan Graham, owner of chocolate brand[Compartés](https://compartes.com/) , highlights the benefits of 24-hour sales. “In the morning when I come in, I’m constantly looking at Shopify—like, what did we sell overnight?” he says on an episode of[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/from-family-shop-to-luxury-chocolate-empire-lessons-from-compartes-chocolate) . The after-hours channel is especially valuable when demand surges unexpectedly, like after a celebrity post about one of the brand’s products: “I go to sleep, I wake up, the next day there were 500 orders on Shopify for peanut butter cups,” he says.


### Reduce overheads


Moving all or part of your business online can help you reduce expenses like retail rent, utilities, business licenses, administrative paperwork, and in-store staffing.


### Get data you can act on


Online sales can generate detailed customer data.[Store analytics](https://www.shopify.com/blog/analyzing-shopify-reports) can reveal how customers browse and buy, where traffic originates, and where shoppers drop off during checkout—information you can use to hone your marketing and refine the[customer experience](https://www.shopify.com/blog/customer-experience-strategy) .


Common metrics to track include[conversion rate](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ecommerce-conversion-rate) ,[average order value](https://www.shopify.com/blog/average-order-value) (AOV),[customer acquisition cost](https://www.shopify.com/blog/customer-acquisition-cost) (CAC), new versus returning customer ratio, and sessions by traffic source. Conversion funnel reports can show you how many site visitors add to cart, reach checkout, and complete a purchase. You can use this data to identify bestsellers and slow movers, prioritize high-performing[marketing channels](https://www.shopify.com/blog/marketing-channels) , and see where customers abandon the journey.


“I actually base a lot of my business decisions on looking at that Shopify data,” Jonathan says, noting that reviewing past orders for particular products through his Shopify admin helps him forecast order quantities for seasonal products like Valentine’s Day heart-shaped boxes.

## How to move your business online


- Outline your business goals
- Choose your platform
- Choose a payment system
- Build your website
- Compile and list your inventory
- Create product descriptions and imagery
- Plan delivery and fulfillment
- Manage customer service
- Build an online marketing strategy


If you’re a store owner looking to make the transition online or open up a digital channel, here’s a list of steps you can follow to make the transition effective:


### Outline your business goals


Forecast how a move online will support your business. Outline specific, measurable goals you wish to meet, like finding new audiences, increasing revenue, or supporting a new business idea.


Then research your target audience’s existing behaviour. Review similar stores’ marketing and product offerings, look at competitors’ customer reviews to identify popular products and common concerns, and survey your in-store customers about their online shopping habits. What are they purchasing online, and how do they buy these products and services? Use this information to determine whether you need to tweak your products, services, or presentation so they work in a digital format.


### Choose your platform


Decide whether to build an independent website or use a third-party platform. The right option depends on the level of functionality you need, your budget, and technical resources:


-


**Independent website.** Building your own site gives you the most control but requires advanced developer knowledge or technical support. It’s the strongest fit if you have a complex custom workflow, an in-house dev team, or highly specific design requirements a template can’t accommodate.


-


**Ecommerce platform.** Platforms like Shopify allow you to plug-and-play, with a[simplified playbook](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/intro-to-shopify/initial-setup/move-an-offine-business-online) for small business owners making an offline-to-online transition. That includes uploading products, adding gift cards, building site pages, setting up payments and shipping, launching marketing, and more. Most also offer a free trial so you can preview functionality before subscribing.


### Choose a payment system


Your online business needs a secure[payment processor](https://www.shopify.com/blog/payment-options) to accept customer transactions. If you’re keeping a physical presence while adding online sales, review the[point-of-sale (POS) system](https://www.shopify.com/blog/point-of-sale-system) and accounting tools already running in your physical store, and check whether they can also operate online.[Shopify POS](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/sell-in-person/shopify-pos/index) , for example, syncs inventory, orders, and customers across in-person and online channels.


Shopify store owners in[39 supported countries](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/supported-countries) —including the US, Canada, Mexico, the UK, most EU countries, Australia, Japan, Singapore, and the UAE—can set up[Shopify Payments](https://www.shopify.com/blog/shopify-payments) to accept online transactions. This system supports major cards like Visa, Mastercard, and American Express, as well as[digital wallets](https://www.shopify.com/blog/digital-wallets) like Apple Pay and Google Pay, without needing a third-party gateway or payment processor. Available payment methods vary by country.


### Build your website


Map out your new website and how customers will move from the homepage to product discovery to checkout. Start by listing pages you need—your homepage, product collections, individual product pages, and delivery and returns information.


You don’t need a sprawling catalog to launch. According to Shopify’s[2026 Entrepreneur Effect report](https://cdn.shopify.com/static/the-entrepreneur-effect/the-entrepreneur-effect-report.pdf) , 41% of Shopify stores open with just one product. Sketch out how your pages will connect via menus or linked collections, and group individual products into clearly named categories so customers can easily find what they need.


Match your in-person branding to your digital branding for uniformity, and register a[domain name](https://www.shopify.com/blog/choose-domain-name) that reflects your business and is[search engine optimization](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ecommerce-seo-beginners-guide) (SEO) friendly. Shopify’s[online store](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/index) tools make it easy to set up themes, add custom domains, and create webpages,[product pages](https://www.shopify.com/blog/product-page) , and linked checkout buttons (no developer required). The Entrepreneur Effect report shows that 78% of Shopify retailers build their own stores, and 86% of surveyed entrepreneurs say ecommerce platforms have made starting a business easier than it was a decade ago.


In a[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/original-duckhead-retail-strategy-breaking-into-the-market) interview, Original Duckhead Founder Morgan Cros shares the importance of a relevant site layout and tailoring your site to how customers prefer to shop. “We quickly realized that we needed to have a better user experience, and that we needed to be mobile first,” she says. All Shopify websites are[responsive](https://www.shopify.com/blog/responsive-web-design) and adapt to users’ devices.


Original Duckhead kept web design costs low by using pre-made Shopify themes and focused on a digital storefront easily viewable on mobile, which is how much of its customer base shops. This switch lifted revenues and checkout completion rates.


### Compile and list your inventory


Decide how your product selection will translate online. For online migration, you have the choice of matching your brick-and-mortar[inventory](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ecommerce-inventory-management) completely, creating a limited product selection, or offering new product listings entirely. Review your sales records to identify bestselling items, then assess which products are suitable for delivery.


Count stock available for sale, and enter accurate quantities for each product and variant. If you’re selling the same inventory online as in person, use an inventory management system that updates quantities across both channels as purchases are made. Shopify store owners can use[Shopify POS](https://www.shopify.com/pos/pos-inventory-system) built-in inventory management to track stock across online and in-person sales that syncs stock increases or decreases.


### Create product descriptions and imagery


In physical stores, customers can inspect items or ask staff for help. On a website, they rely on the images, videos, and descriptions on product pages to guide their selections. Ensure that your descriptions are thorough, accurate, and detailed. Mention size, dimensions, materials, contents, ingredients, allergens, and warranty information where relevant, and add high-quality images.


Jonathan of Compartés considered how to retain the same informative, vivid experience for customers when transitioning from retail to a solely ecommerce store. “Thinking through the design of a store, the smell of the store, the displays of the store, how does that translate onto our Shopify side?” he says. “Making sure we have beautiful, vivid imagery that captures the chocolate in a luxurious light … making that online shopping experience just as great for them that they can do it from their phones, computers, at their desks has been huge.”


### Plan delivery and fulfillment


Plan how your product will reach customers and[calculate shipping](https://www.shopify.com/blog/common-shipping-questions) and packaging costs. Check each product’s weight, dimensions, fragility, and storage requirements. Compare shipping options based on delivery times and handling needs, and note any required preparation, packaging, and shipping materials.


Make sure your product range is safe for transit and well protected. Food, fragile items, and temperature-sensitive goods may need specialist packaging or limited delivery areas. Send a trial package to confirm items arrive in good condition and within expected delivery windows.


Assess what areas you can realistically serve and whether shipping costs stay reasonable for customers without eating into your margins. Compare carrier coverage, delivery estimates, and quotes for packed orders, then calculate how much of this cost you can absorb while maintaining profit. Map how your workflow will operate for digital orders—how your team will receive, pack, dispatch, and track items, and how you’ll display shipping options, costs, and times clearly on your website.


If you’re keeping a brick-and-mortar store, you can also offer in-person fulfillment options like click and collect. Shopify’s[Shipping setup](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/fulfillment/setup/shipping-rates) supports flat, conditional, carrier-calculated, and local delivery rates.


### Manage customer service


Online customers can’t always ask a staff member a question before buying. Establish clear support channels for queries, feedback, and communication—like a contact section, an FAQ page, automated chat, or a monitored email inbox. Include your time zone, location, and customer service hours if you use live support.


If you’re keeping a physical location, update your[Google Business Profile](https://www.shopify.com/blog/google-business-profile) and listings on platforms like Yelp, Bing Places, and Apple Business Connect so customers can find accurate opening hours, contact details, and website links. Add a short description explaining your fulfillment options, including any delivery or in-store pickup services, and keep these listings updated as things change.


### Build an online marketing strategy


Identify the customers you want to reach with your online store, then research your target demographic using customer surveys, existing sales data, or online research into competitor models to understand your audience’s interests, shopping habits, and preferred channels.


Tell existing customers about your online business through your current email list, social media pages, and in-store signage. Explain how to order and highlight available delivery or pickup options, and coordinate promotions across channels to make any differences in offers or shopping capabilities clear.


At the same time, focus on reaching new customers interested in your products. Your digital marketing strategy could involve[email newsletters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/email-newsletter) , paid marketing like Google ads and[social media ads](https://www.shopify.com/blog/social-media-advertising) , blogs and[content marketing](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-content-marketing) , SEO, and AI optimization (AIO). For example, you can publish content answering common product questions to attract search traffic, or run digital ads aimed at customers in areas where you deliver.


Wellness brand[Free Soul](https://freesoul.com/) ’s founder Arjun Sofat used email marketing and paid media when building his brand online, putting money into ads on Facebook and Google. “You need to think wider than your immediate circle,” he says on *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/free-soul-creative-customer-aquisition-strategies)* . “You quickly realize that the network of people that can buy your products and benefit from your brand probably sits outside of your immediate circle.”


## How to move your business online FAQ


### How do I move a business online?


To move your business online, start by defining your goals, choosing your ecommerce platform and payment system, and building your website. Prepare your inventory, establish your delivery and customer service processes, then create a digital marketing strategy to take your business to launch.


### How can I combine online and in-person sales?


Combine online and in-person sales by using a system that connects your ecommerce store with your physical POS. Tools like Shopify and Shopify POS can sync inventory, orders, and customer information across both channels.


### How can you grow your business online for free?


To grow your business without paying for ads, use free digital marketing tactics like publishing content optimized for search engines, building organic reach on social media platforms, showcasing customer reviews and positive feedback, and promoting your store through in-store signage.
